idiom_name: if (bad) throw/return; Objects.requireNonNull for argument guards
implementation_notes: Java guards are if plus throw or return; the standard library supplies the fail-fast helpers - Objects.requireNonNull(obj) / requireNonNull(obj, message) for null arguments and Objects.checkIndex/checkFromToIndex for range arguments - which replace the hand-written null-check-and-throw block and keep the happy path flat. The assert statement is disabled unless the JVM runs with -ea, so it documents invariants during development and never validates caller input. Pattern matching (instanceof patterns and switch guards) keeps the admission checks compact without nesting.
pitfalls: assert is off by default (-ea enables it) and must never stand in for argument checks that must always run.
A guard that mutates before failing (adding to a collection, setting a field) leaves partially applied state; check before the first mutation.
Checked exceptions thrown by a guard widen every caller signature; precondition violations in the JDK style are unchecked (IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, NullPointerException).
